messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 51
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Welder
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
- Pcl5: 52

He is 51, a married man from Oceania who has spent most of his adult life working as a welder. Before the crash, he thinks of himself as steady, practical, and used to hard conditions. He likes work that is physical and exact. He trusts his hands, his routine, and the predictability of metal: measure, cut, heat, join. He is not someone who used to talk much about feelings. His wife says that before everything changed, he was tired after work but easy to be around, always ready to fix something around the house or drive out with family on the weekend.

The collision happens on an ordinary workday before sunrise. He is driving his utility truck along a familiar road, heading to a fabrication site with his tools in the back. The weather is poor and the road is slick. He remembers seeing headlights where they should not be, bright and sudden, then the violent impact. Later he can describe the sound more clearly than the images: metal crushing inward, glass exploding, the engine screaming. In the first moments after the crash, he cannot understand why he cannot move properly. He smells petrol, tastes blood, and is certain the vehicle will catch fire. He thinks, very plainly, I am going to die here. He hears another driver shouting somewhere outside, but the sound seems far away, as if he is underwater. He is trapped long enough for panic to turn into something colder. He keeps trying to pull air in, waiting for another hit, another explosion.

He survives with orthopedic injuries and bruising, but what stays with him most is the feeling of helplessness inside the cab. In the hospital he tells people he is lucky. He says others have had worse. He wants to get home, sleep in his own bed, and get back to work. For a little while he believes that if he keeps moving, the whole thing will settle by itself.

Instead, the crash begins to follow him. At night he wakes suddenly, heart pounding, soaked in sweat, his body tense before he is fully conscious. Sometimes he has the same dream: headlights rushing at him and no space to turn. Sometimes there is no image at all, only the sensation of being pinned and unable to breathe. His wife learns not to touch him unexpectedly when he is asleep because he comes up swinging or shoves her away before he knows where he is. In the morning he feels ashamed and exhausted.

As his physical injuries improve, he expects himself to resume normal life, but driving becomes its own ordeal. He grips the steering wheel until his hands ache. If a car drifts near the center line, his chest tightens and he feels a jolt of heat through his whole body. He starts taking longer routes to avoid the stretch of road where the collision happened. Eventually he refuses that road entirely. If rain starts while he is out, he turns back or pulls over until it passes. He tells himself he is being sensible, but the world has started to feel full of traps.

Returning to welding is harder than he admits. At the workshop, the noise of dropped steel or the sudden hiss of pressure release can make him flinch so sharply that the younger men glance over. Once, when a forklift backfires outside, he drops his torch and crouches before he can stop himself. He laughs it off, but afterward he sits in the crib room pretending to check messages while his heart races. He used to enjoy the focus of fabrication, but now his concentration slips. He rereads measurements, loses track of steps, and worries about making mistakes that could injure someone. By the end of the day he is wrung out from holding himself together.

At home he is less patient than he used to be. Small noises irritate him. He snaps at his wife for leaving late, then feels guilty and withdraws. He spends more time alone in the shed, tinkering without finishing anything. Family gatherings feel noisy and crowded; he sits where he can see the exits and leaves early if he can. People ask how he is and he gives the same answer—fine, just tired—because the truth feels both too large and somehow undeserved. He knows he lived. He knows he should be grateful.

What troubles him most is how unfamiliar he feels to himself. He used to believe that fear belonged to the moment of danger and then passed. Now it arrives in safe places: in traffic lights, in the crunch of tires on wet road, in a flash of reflected headlights across the lounge room wall. Some days he can almost manage his old rhythm. Other days his body reacts before his mind catches up, and he is back inside the wreckage, waiting for impact or fire. He wants badly to be the man who just gets on with things, but more and more of his energy goes into avoiding reminders, controlling his temper, and hiding how shaken he still is. His wife sees the distance in him. He sees it too, and that recognition frightens him nearly as much as the crash itself.
